oneLineAnswer: A prescription medicine that treats high blood pressure in the lungs, given only under strict liver and pregnancy monitoring.
whatItIs: Bosentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist, meaning it blocks the receptors that the protein endothelin docks into. The FDA label calls it a highly substituted pyrimidine derivative with no chiral centers. The label describes the drug substance as bosentan monohydrate, and its tablet ingredient list names bosentan anhydrous, which is the same molecule without an attached water unit. PubChem records bosentan's formula as C27H29N5O6S with a weight of 551.6, while the label's monohydrate form weighs 569.64.
whatItDoes: The FDA label says bosentan treats pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), which is high blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs.
In adults, the label says it aims to improve exercise ability and to reduce clinical worsening.
In children aged 3 and older, the label says it aims to improve pulmonary vascular resistance.
The label states bosentan works by blocking endothelin receptor types A and B, and notes that endothelin-1 levels are raised in the lungs of people with PAH.
The label records that it comes as tablets taken by mouth, or as tablets that dissolve in water for children.
howPeopleUseIt: On the label it is a prescription medicine for people already diagnosed with PAH, not a general blood pressure treatment.
The label says it is dispensed only through a restricted program called the Bosentan REMS, and that prescribers, patients and pharmacies must all enroll.
The label requires liver enzyme blood tests before treatment starts and then once a month, because the medicine carries a liver risk.
ClinicalTrials.gov lists bosentan studies in other conditions, such as skin fibrosis in systemic sclerosis; those are research settings, not labeled uses.

commonSideEffects: In trials, the most common effects were respiratory tract infections, headache and swelling called edema.
The label also lists chest pain, fainting, flushing, low blood pressure, sinusitis, joint pain, a pounding heartbeat and anemia.
Rises in liver enzymes above three times normal were seen in about 11% of treated patients versus 2% on placebo.
Hemoglobin and red blood cell counts can fall, so the label asks for checks after 1 and 3 months and then every 3 months.
seriousSigns: The label carries a boxed warning for liver injury, and says liver failure has been reported.
The label tells patients to stop and get help for nausea, vomiting, fever, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or unusual tiredness.
Fluid retention can develop, and the label says some patients needed a diuretic, fluid management, or hospital care for heart failure.
Rare allergic reactions include DRESS, anaphylaxis, rash and swelling of the lips.
The label says hemoglobin falls that are large enough to need a transfusion have been reported after the drug reached the market.
In one small safety study, sperm counts dropped by at least half in about a quarter of the men taking part.
whoShouldAvoid: The label says do not use bosentan if you are pregnant.
Do not use it with cyclosporine A, or with the diabetes medicine glyburide; the label lists both combinations as contraindicated.
Do not use it if you are allergic to bosentan, including past DRESS, anaphylaxis, rash or lip swelling.
The label says it should generally be avoided in people whose liver enzymes are already above three times normal.
Women who could become pregnant must use reliable contraception and add a second method, because hormonal birth control alone may not be dependable on this medicine.
The label advises women not to breastfeed while taking it.

interactions: Hormonal birth control may not work reliably; the label reports average drops of 31% in ethinyl estradiol and 14% in norethindrone, and falls as large as 66% in individual users.
Cyclosporine A sharply raises bosentan levels in the blood, and the label makes that combination a contraindication.

The label does not recommend pairing bosentan with a CYP2C9 inhibitor such as fluconazole together with a strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitor such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin or diltiazem.
Bosentan speeds up two liver enzymes, CYP3A and CYP2C9, so it lowers levels of other drugs broken down by them; the label names statins such as simvastatin, warfarin and rifampin.
The label gives special handling instructions for people taking ritonavir, an HIV medicine.
Ketoconazole raised bosentan blood levels by roughly 100% in healthy volunteers, according to the label.
pregnancyAndChildren: The label makes pregnancy a contraindication, because animal reproduction studies found fetal harm. In rats, a dose twice the maximum recommended human dose on a body-surface basis caused malformations of the head, mouth, face and large blood vessels. The label says human data from similar drugs have not shown a clear increase in major birth defects, but those reports are limited and lack control groups. The label advises women who could become pregnant to test for pregnancy first, use effective contraception during treatment, and keep using it for one month after the last dose. Bosentan passes into breast milk, and the label advises choosing between breastfeeding and the medicine. For children, the label covers patients aged 3 and older with idiopathic or congenital PAH, and says the safety profile in 119 children resembled that in adults.
whatWeDoNotKnow: The label says the available human data cannot confirm or rule out a link between bosentan and major birth defects, because the reports lack control groups and details on dose and timing.
The label states that the clinical impact of blocking both endothelin receptor types is unknown.
Effects in severe liver impairment have not been evaluated, per the label.
There is little information on bosentan's effect on milk production, or on how it affects a breastfed baby.
Trial safety data covered exposures of up to about 4.1 years, so longer-term outcomes are less well described.
No public-domain source was found for how many people take bosentan, or for its cost or availability outside the United States.

gaps: NCCIH has no bosentan page; https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/bosentan returned 404, so no supplement-style source exists for this substance.
LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547999/) blocked automated access behind a browser check, so no independent liver-injury reference is cited here.

openFDA has no label indexed under the generic name Bosentan Anhydrous; searches by that name returned no results. The anhydrous substance appears inside the Tracleer label's ingredient listing and in PubChem.
The DailyMed single-label JSON endpoint rejected the request, so label content was taken from the DailyMed HTML page and the openFDA label record instead.
No public-domain source covered how many people take bosentan, its price, or its availability outside the United States.
MedlinePlus drug monographs for bosentan were deliberately not used because they are licensed, copyrighted content.
summary: Covers what bosentan is, the pulmonary arterial hypertension it is labeled to treat, its liver and pregnancy risks, common side effects, interactions, and the limits of what the label establishes.
